exec: FAA has halted its router replacement after the ground stop; no cyberattack indicated.
impact: More than 9,100 flights were canceled, according to FlightAware as cited by Fox Weather; about 3,500 flights were in the air at the time.
plain: A flood of data from newly installed routers knocked out US air traffic communications on November 13. The FAA has now stopped installing those routers and gone back to its old ones while the fault is studied.

key_findings: A data flood on the FAA FTI network, about 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, destabilised legacy equipment and disrupted aircraft communications and radar feeds.
Instability began at 17 of 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers and spread to several TRACON facilities; radio frequencies and some radar feeds stayed up.
Preliminary sources are a radar site in Amarillo, Texas and a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where L3Harris was deploying a new router.
The FAA says all available evidence shows no indication of a cyberattack or outside malicious actor.
Operators cancelled about 12,462 flights, 9,082 by major airlines; around 3,500 airborne aircraft landed safely.
recommendations: The FAA disabled the affected function on the originating Juniper routers and on more than 60 others, and paused further installations.
The broadcasting function was disabled on all new routers as a precaution.
The FAA will reevaluate when maintenance is performed, since this router replacement was done midday at a remote facility.

sources.name: BNN Bloomberg / CTV News live updates (AP)

summary: Legacy FAA equipment became unstable on November 13 when data flooded its FTI network, disrupting 17 of 22 en route centers. AP reports the FAA has paused installing the new routers linked to the failure and switched off Juniper units already installed, relying on old Cisco routers while L3Harris tests the faulty units. Fox Weather says the ground stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m. Friday. The FAA sees no indication of a cyberattack.
title: FAA grounds all US departures after air traffic communications failure
